*   [April 11](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/11_aprile?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "April 11th") – [Torvaianica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Torvaianica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Torvaianica") ( [Rome](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Roma?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Rome") ): The lifeless body of twenty-three-year-old [Wilma Montesi](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Caso_Montesi?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Montesi Case") is found on the beach . Investigations into her death reveal her association with numerous young men from Rome's upper classes, sparking a massive political scandal. The murder remains unsolved.

Ritornerà soltanto nel [1972](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/1972?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "1972"), per ritirare il [Premio Oscar alla carriera](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Oscar_onorario?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Honorary Oscar").
*   [22 aprile](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/22_aprile?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "April 22nd") – sbarca a [Napoli](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Napoli?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Naples"), [Clare Boothe Luce](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Clare_Boothe_Luce?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Clare Boothe Luce"), nuova [ambasciatrice](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Ambasciatore?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Ambassador") degli Stati Uniti in Italia.
*   [25 aprile](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/25_aprile?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "April 25th") – [James Watson](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/James_Dewey_Watson?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "James Dewey Watson") e [Francis Crick](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Francis_Crick?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Francis Crick") pubblicano sulla rivista _[Nature](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Nature?\_x\_tr\_sl=it&\_x\_tr\_tl=en&\_x\_tr\_hl=en "Nature")_ la loro ricerca che descrive la struttura a [doppia elica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Doppia_elica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Double helix") dell'acido desossiribonucleico, il [DNA](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/DNA?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "DNA").

### Giugno

[modifica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/w/index.php?title=1953&action=edit&section=7&_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Edit the June section")

*   [7](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/7_giugno?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "June 7th")-[8 giugno](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/8_giugno?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "June 8th") – [elezioni politiche](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Elezioni_politiche_in_Italia_del_1953?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "1953 Italian general election") in Italia: la coalizione di centro ([Democrazia Cristiana](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Democrazia_Cristiana?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Christian Democracy"), [PSDI](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Partito_Socialista_Democratico_Italiano?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Italian Democratic Socialist Party"), [PLI](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Partito_Liberale_Italiano?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Italian Liberal Party") e [PRI](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Partito_Repubblicano_Italiano?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Italian Republican Party")) non riesce a ottenere la [maggioranza assoluta](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Maggioranza?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Majority"), si ferma al 49,85%, non scatta quindi il premio di maggioranza assicurato dalla [legge truffa](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Legge_elettorale_italiana_del_1953?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Italian electoral law of 1953").
*   [17 giugno](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/17_giugno?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "June 17th") – [Berlino Est](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Berlino_Est?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "East Berlin"): [carri armati](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Carro_armato?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Tank") sovietici intervengono contro gli operai che [dimostrano](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Moti_operai_del_1953_nella_Germania_Est?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Workers' riots in East Germany in 1953") contro le nuove e più pesanti norme di lavoro.
*   [19 giugno](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/19_giugno?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "June 19th") – [Penitenziario di Sing Sing](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Sing_Sing?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Sing Sing"), [New York](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/New_York?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "New York"): i coniugi comunisti di origine [ebraica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Ebrei?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Jews")[Julius ed Ethel Rosenberg](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Caso_Rosenberg?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Rosenberg case"), accusati di [spionaggio](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Spionaggio?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Espionage"), sono giustiziati sulla [sedia elettrica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Sedia_elettrica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Electric chair"). Il loro caso aveva sollevato grande eco e manifestazioni di protesta in tutto il mondo.

*   [12 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/12_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 12th") – [Unione Sovietica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Unione_Sovietica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Soviet Union"): nel poligono di [Semipalatinsk](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Semej?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Semej") esplode la prima bomba atomica "mista" a [fissione](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Fissione_nucleare?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Nuclear fission")-[fusione](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Fusione_nucleare?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Nuclear fusion"), venti volte più potente di quella sganciata a [Hiroshima](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Hiroshima?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Hiroshima").
*   [12 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/12_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 12th") – [Grecia](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Grecia?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Greece"): [terremoto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Terremoto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Earthquake") delle [isole Ionie](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Isole_Ionie?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Ionian Islands").
*   [17 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/17_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 17th") – [Giuseppe Pella](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Giuseppe_Pella?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Joseph Pella") è il nuovo [Presidente del Consiglio dei ministri](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Presidente_del_Consiglio_dei_ministri_della_Repubblica_Italiana?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "President of the Council of Ministers of the Italian Republic").
*   [27 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/27_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 27") – firma del concordato tra [Santa Sede](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Santa_Sede?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Holy See") e governo spagnolo
*   [29 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/29_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 29") – [1º settembre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/1%C2%BA_settembre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "September 1st"): lacrimazione miracolosa di un quadretto di gesso raffigurante il [Cuore Immacolato di Maria](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Cuore_Immacolato_di_Maria?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Immaculate Heart of Mary") a [Siracusa](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Siracusa?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Syracuse"), conosciuto oggi con l'appellativo di [Madonna delle Lacrime](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Madonna_delle_Lacrime?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Our Lady of Tears").
*   [30 agosto](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/30_agosto?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "August 30th") – [Fausto Coppi](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Fausto_Coppi?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Fausto Coppi") conquista il titolo mondiale di [ciclismo su strada](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Ciclismo_su_strada?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Road cycling") a [Lugano](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Lugano?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Lugano").

### Settembre

[modifica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/w/index.php?title=1953&action=edit&section=10&_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Edit the September section")

*   [7 settembre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/7_settembre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "September 7th") – [Unione Sovietica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Unione_Sovietica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Soviet Union"): in seguito alla morte di [Stalin](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Iosif_Stalin?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Joseph Stalin"), dopo un periodo di gestione collettiva, [Chruščëv](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Nikita_Sergeevi%C4%8D_Chru%C5%A1%C4%8D%C3%ABv?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Nikita Sergeevich Khrushchev") diventa [segretario](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Segretario_generale_del_PCUS?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "General Secretary of the CPSU") del Comitato Centrale del [Partito Comunista dell'Unione Sovietica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Partito_Comunista_dell'Unione_Sovietica?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Communist Party of the Soviet Union") (PCUS).
*   [16 settembre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/16_settembre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "September 16th") – [Stati Uniti d'America](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Stati_Uniti_d'America?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "United States of America"): per la prima volta viene proiettato un film in [Cinemascope](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/CinemaScope?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "CinemaScope"). Si tratta di _[The robe](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/La\_tunica?\_x\_tr\_sl=it&\_x\_tr\_tl=en&\_x\_tr\_hl=en "The tunic")_ (_La tunica_), prodotto dalla [20th Century Fox](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/20th_Century_Fox?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "20th Century Fox"), per la regia di [Henry Koster](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Henry_Koster?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Henry Koster").

### Ottobre

[modifica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/w/index.php?title=1953&action=edit&section=11&_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Edit the October section")

*   [8 ottobre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/8_ottobre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "October 8th") – i governi [statunitense](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Governo_federale_degli_Stati_Uniti_d'America?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Federal Government of the United States of America") e [britannico](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Governo_di_Sua_Maest%C3%A0?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "His Majesty's Government") annunciano simultaneamente (la cosiddetta _nota bipartita_) la fine del governo militare alleato a [Trieste](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Trieste?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Trieste"), il ritiro delle truppe dalla zona A del [Territorio libero](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Territorio_Libero_di_Trieste?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Free Territory of Trieste") e la sua rimessione all'amministrazione italiana.
*   [10 ottobre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/10_ottobre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "October 10th") – in risposta alla _nota bipartita_ angloamericana dell'8 ottobre, il leader [jugoslavo](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Jugoslavia?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Yugoslavia"), [maresciallo Tito](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Josip_Broz_Tito?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Josip Broz Tito"), minaccia di occupare militarmente la zona A del Territorio Libero di Trieste.
*   [21 ottobre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/21_ottobre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "October 21st") – [Calabria](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Calabria?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Calabria"): un forte nubifragio provoca [alluvioni](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Alluvione?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Flood") nelle province di [Reggio Calabria](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Provincia_di_Reggio_Calabria?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Province of Reggio Calabria") e [Catanzaro](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/Provincia_di_Catanzaro?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Province of Catanzaro"). Oltre cento le vittime.

### Dicembre

[modifica](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/w/index.php?title=1953&action=edit&section=13&_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "Edit the December section")

*   [30 dicembre](https://it-wikipedia-org.translate.goog/wiki/30_dicembre?_x_tr_sl=it&_x_tr_tl=en&_x_tr_hl=en "December 30th") – USA - Viene messo sul mercato il primo televisore a colori.

## Today in Music History: Remembering Leonard Cohen

November 07, 2017

Save

![Image 3: Leonard Cohen's new album, Popular Problems, comes out Sept. 23.](https://img.apmcdn.org/de274a40ecad912fd2968def061b4de6f8b32cd9/uncropped/75e62c-20140915-leonard-cohen.jpg)

Leonard Cohen's new album, Popular Problems, comes out Sept. 23.Courtesy the artist

**History Highlight:**

Today in 2016, Canadian singer, songwriter and poet Leonard Cohen died at the age of 82 at his home in Los Angeles. Cohen pursued a career as a poet and novelist during the 1950s and early 1960s, and did not launch a music career until 1967, at the age of 33. His first album, _Songs of Leonard Cohen_ (1967), was followed by three more albums of folk music: _Songs from a Room_, _Songs of Love and Hate_ and _New Skin for the Old Ceremony_. "Hallelujah" is a song written by Cohen, originally released on his album _Various Positions_. The song found greater popular acclaim through a recording by John Cale, which inspired a recording by Jeff Buckley.

**Today In:**

1951 - Frank Sinatra married his second wife, actress Ava Gardner. The couple split up in 1953 and divorced in 1957. Sinatra was married three other times - to his first wife Nancy Barbato, to the actress Mia Farrow and finally to Barbara Marx, to whom he was married at his death.

1958 - Eddie Cochran made his U.K. chart debut with "Summertime Blues". It reached No.18 in the U.K. & No.8 in the U.S. The song has been covered by many artists, including being a No. 1 hit for country singer Alan Jackson and a notable hit for The Who.

1963 - The Beatles went to Ireland to make their only two appearances ever in the country playing two shows at the Adelphi Cinema, Dublin.

1967 - The Beatles finished recording "Blue Jay Way", "Flying" and "Magical Mystery Tour".

1968 - After Jim Morrison exhorted the audience to stand up at a concert, The Doors were banned in Phoenix because the local authorities were nervous. He had recently mooned an audience at another concert.

1969 - The Rolling Stones opened their first U.S. concert tour in three years. By this time they were notorious bad boys after tales of drug busts, censorship battles and wild life on the road, so the tour had become a full-blown media circus.

1974 - Ted Nugent won the National Squirrel Shooting Archery Contest by hitting a squirrel at 150 yards with a bow and arrow.  
  
1975 - A new world record was set for continuous guitar string plucking by a guy named Steve Anderson, who played for 114 hours 17 minutes.

1975 - Elton John started a three-week run at No. 1 on the U.S. album chart with _Rock Of The Westies_, the singer's tenth studio album and seventh U.S. No. 1.

1977 - the soundtrack to _Saturday Night Fever_ was released. The film has been citied as the first example of "cross-media marketing", with the tie-in soundtrack's single being used to help promote the film _before_ its release and the film popularizing the entire soundtrack _after_ its release.

1981 - Hall and Oates started a two-week run at No. 1 on the U.S. singles chart with "Private Eyes", the duo's third U.S. No. 1, a No. 32 hit in the U.K.

1987 - Tiffany became the youngest act to score a U.S. No. 1 since Michael Jackson ("Ben", in 1972) with "I Think We're Alone Now". The song written by Ritchie Cordell was initially a 1967 hit for Tommy James & the Shondells. Fun fact: Tiffany hated the idea of recording a version of her own for her album because she thought the song wasn't modern or hip enough.

2014 - Two wealthy fans paid $300,000 to eat lasagne with Bruce Springsteen at his house. Springsteen started off the annual Stand Up For Heroes event by playing an acoustic set, then offering the instrument to the highest bidder. When bidding reached $60,000, he threw in a guitar lesson, which someone offered $250,000 for. At this point, he offered up a lasagne dinner at his house, a ride around the block in the sidecar of his motorbike and the shirt off of his back. All the money went to the Bob Woodruff Foundation, which helps injured servicemen and their families when they return home.

**Birthdays:**

Joni Mitchell is 74.

Robin Finck of Nine Inch Nails and Guns N' Roses is 46.

Lorde is 21.

_Highlights for Today in Music History are gathered from_ _[This Day in Music](link_16)_ _,_ _[Paul Shaffer's Day in Rock](link_17)_ _,_ _[Song Facts](link_18)_ _and_ _[Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Main\_Page)_ _._

## October 4th

2023 - Lady Gaga

 A US judge ruled that [Lady Gaga](link_21) would not have to pay a $500,000 (£410,000) reward to a woman who returned her dogs after they were stolen in 2021. Jennifer McBride previously sued the star for the "no questions asked" reward, plus $1.5m (£1.2m) in damages. But the judge said Ms McBride couldn't claim the money because her role in returning the star's dogs had led to a conviction of receiving stolen goods. 

2022 - Loretta Lynn

 American country music singer and songwriter Loretta Lynn died at the age of 90. She was the first woman to be named Country Music Artist Entertainer Of The Year. Since her first No.1 'Fist City', in 1967 she has scored another 16 chart toppers. Lynn wrote more than 160 songs and released 60 albums and won three Grammy Awards. Her best-selling 1976 autobiography was made into an Academy Award-winning film, Coal Miner's Daughter, starring Sissy Spacek and Tommy Lee Jones in 1980. 

2019 - Abbey Road

 The Beatles' [Abbey Road](link_22) returned to No.1 in the UK, 50 years after it first topped the album charts after the release of an expanded anniversary edition. The feat also sees the album set a record - the gap of 49 years and 252 days since its initial chart-topping run ended in early 1970 is the longest gap before returning to No.1. 

2014 - Paul Revere

 Paul Revere, organist and leader of Paul Revere And The Raiders died following a battle with cancer. Between 1961 and 1971, the band placed 15 songs on Billboard's Top 40, including the US Top 10 hits 'Kicks', 'Hungry', 'Good Thing' and 'Him Or Me - What's It Gonna Be?' 

2008 - Darius Rucker

 Darius Rucker former singer with Hootie & the Blowfish went to No.1 on the US Country chart with his first country single, 'Don't Think I Don't Think About It,' making him the first African American singer to top the chart since 1985, when [Ray Charles](link_23) hit the top with 'Seven Spanish Angels,' a duet with [Willie Nelson](link_24). 

2007 - Phil Spector

 Producer [Phil Spector](link_25) was set to be retried for the murder of actress Lana Clarkson following the collapse of the first trial in Sept of this year. The first trial ended with the jury deadlocked 10-2 favouring conviction. Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Larry Paul Fidler set another hearing for the case on 23 October. 

2007 - The Rolling Stones

 The [Rolling Stones](link_26) set a new record for the top grossing tour of all time with their A Bigger Bang tour. The tour which ran from late 2005 to August 2007, earned the band £247m, ($437m) with The Stones playing to over 3.5 million people at 113 shows. The previous high was set by [U2](link_27)'s Vertigo tour, which took place in 2005 and 2006, earning £220m, ($389m). 

[Video 1](link_28)

2006 - R Kelly

 Former R Kelly employee (who claimed to have been a ‘mentor and guide’ to Kelly since he was a teenager) Henry Vaughn filed a lawsuit against the singer accusing him of assault, false imprisonment, and a breach of contract that defrauded him of songwriting royalties. Vaughn also claimed that Kelly and his associates dragged him to the basement at Kelly’s Olympia Fields home and ‘repeatedly struck him about the face and body with his fists. 

2005 - Mike Gibbins

 Welsh musician Mike Gibbins and drummer with [Badfinger](link_29) died in his sleep at his Florida home aged 56. Badfinger had the 1970 UK No.4 & US No.7 single 'Come And Get It' and enjoyed success with other hit songs 'No Matter What', 'Day After Day', and 'Baby Blue'. During his tenure with Badfinger, Gibbins - along with the other members of the band - contributed musically to the George Harrison album [All Things Must Pass](link_30), and played at The Concert for Bangladesh. He had also been a member of The Iveys during the 60s. 

[Video 2](link_31)

2000 - Craig David

 UK R&B vocalist Craig David won a record three MasterCard Music of Black Origin (MOBO) Awards at London's Alexandra Palace. He was named Best UK Newcomer and won awards for Best R&B Act and Best UK Single for 'Fill Me In.'

# How Facebook uses the email or mobile phone number on your profile

Copy link

 We’re gradually updating people to [Meta Accounts](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.meta.com%2Fhelp%2Fmeta-account%2F876751767182450%3Fhelpref%3Dfaq_content&h=AUCcye1HKMucAy8levGg79-uFE1OhurtHnPhKHSNRqYdLlJmQ0V67jBbeZq0Dqk6vV1G-xzMNGdxe64WLhRXkKV5vcfxHClH1oq2GkENVM5X6owyQzrfVGruYbCPIqTRHzkNPe6Ue-Db7g). You may see either Accounts Center or Meta Account settings as the place to manage your account settings.

## How we use your email address or mobile phone number

We may use your email address or mobile phone number for purposes like:

*   [Helping you log in](https://www.facebook.com/help/283100488694834?helpref=faq_content). If you forget your password, you'll need an updated phone number or email address to reset it. If you forget or [lose access](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content) to the email address or phone number associated with your account, you can use one to look up the other. 
*   Sending you email, WhatsApp and SMS notifications for updates about activity on your account, promotions and account safety. These notifications can help keep your account safe through features like two-factor authentication and alerts about unrecognized logins.
*   Providing and improving ads for you and others. We use your contact information alongside information we get from your activity to help us improve our ads services for everyone within the Facebook community.
*   Some of our security checkpoints can be difficult to pass using assistive technology. If you add a mobile number or email address to your Facebook account, you'll have another way to verify your account if you need to pass any of these checkpoints. Keep in mind that these checkpoints may require internet access. 

By entering your phone number, you authorize your mobile network provider to share data from your account and device to Facebook or its service providers for phone number verification and fraud prevention purposes. Learn more about the data we collect and how we use it in our [Privacy Policy](https://www.facebook.com/privacy/policy/).

We never sell personal information, including your email address and phone number, to anyone. Keep in mind that you can control who can [see your contact information](https://www.facebook.com/help/117118145038822?helpref=faq_content) and who we can [suggest your profile to](https://www.facebook.com/help/131297846947406?helpref=faq_content) based on your phone number or email address. Learn more about how Facebook uses your phone number and email address in our [Privacy Policy.](https://www.facebook.com/about/privacy)

You may see an email or phone number suggested for you when we ask you to add your contact information. Emails or phone numbers shown in this way will only be added to your account if you choose to [add them](https://www.facebook.com/help/223900927622502?helpref=faq_content).

## How we suggest email addresses or phone numbers

We may suggest an email address or phone number for you based on information we receive from sources such as: 

*   Contact information provided by others on Facebook.
*   An email address or phone number that you entered previously but didn't confirm.
*   Your mobile phone or tablet.

## Reasons for confirming your mobile phone number

We may ask you to confirm your mobile phone number because:

*   You previously [added the phone number](https://www.facebook.com/help/297947214257999?helpref=faq_content) we're asking you to confirm.
*   Time has passed since you last added or updated your phone number.
*   We’ve received information from your device that helps us suggest the number connected to that device.
*   You haven’t added one yet, and we want to show you how.

## More information

*   [Add or remove a mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/124895950923762?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Add or remove an email address.](https://www.facebook.com/help/162801153783275?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Adjust how you get notifications.](https://www.facebook.com/help/390022341057202?helpref=faq_content)
*   [Recover your Facebook account if you can't access your account email address or mobile phone number.](https://www.facebook.com/help/132243923516844?helpref=faq_content)

## October 4th

1991 - Leigh-Anne Pinnock

 English singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock. She rose to prominence as a member of the girl group Little Mix, which was formed and won the eighth series of, The X Factor UK. As part of the group, she won three Brit Awards and achieved 19 top-ten singles and five No.1 hits on the UK Singles Chart. 

1985 - Shontelle

 Barbadian singer and songwriter Shontelle Layne, known professionally as Shontelle, who had the 2009 UK top 10 single ‘T-Shirt’. Shontelle was also Beyoncé's opening act for her I Am... World Tour 2009 our during the British leg. 

1984 - Katina Sergeevna

 Katina Sergeevna, singer, with the Russian music duo Tatu, who scored the 2003 UK No.1 single 'All The Things She Said'. The duo represented Russia in the Eurovision Song Contest 2003 with the song 'Ne Ver', Ne Boysia', finishing third. 

1977 - Richard Reed Parry

 Richard Reed Parry, Canadian multi-instrumentalist, composer, producer, best known as a core member of the Grammy Award-winning indie rock band Arcade Fire who had the 2005 album Funeral, and 2017 US No.1 album Everything Now. 

1973 - M. Ward

 American singer-songwriter, M. Ward. He has released 10 studio albums since 1999, and in addition to his solo work, he is a member of indie pop duo She & Him and folk-rock supergroup Monsters of Folk. She & Him's second album, Volume Two, (2010) peaked at No. 6 on the Billboard chart. 

1971 - Darren Middleton

 Australian musician Darren Middleton best known as the lead guitarist and songwriter for alternative rock band Powderfinger. The group's third studio album, Internationalist peaked at No. 1 on the ARIA Albums Chart in September 1998. 

1965 - Neil Sims

 Neil Sims, drummer with English alternative rock band Catherine Wheel. The band was active from 1990 to 2000, releasing five full-length albums in their career. 

1961 - Jon Secada

 Cuban-born American singer, songwriter, actor and record producer Jon Secada. In 1991, Secada co-wrote and was a backup singer for 'Coming Out of the Dark', a No.1 hit song inspired by a tour-bus accident involving Gloria Estefan in 1990, in which her back was broken. In 1992, he released his self-titled debut album, which sold 7 million copies. 

1959 - Chris Lowe

 English musician, songwriter, and co-founder of the synth-pop duo Pet Shop Boys, which he formed with Neil Tennant in 1981. They had the 1986 UK & US No.1 single 'West End Girls', plus three other UK No.1 singles. They have sold more than 100 million records worldwide and have achieved 42 top 30 singles, including 22 top-10 hits on the UK singles chart. In 2024, they were awarded the Pop Pioneers award at the [MTV](https://www.thisdayinmusic.com/liner-notes/i-want-my-mtv) Europe Music Awards. 

1957 - Barbara Kooyman

 American singer-songwriter Barbara Kooyman from the American rock band Timbuk 3. With her then-husband Pat MacDonald, and a drum machine, Timbuk 3, whose 1986 signature song was 'The Future's So Bright, I Gotta Wear Shades'. 

1952 - Jody Stephens

 American musician and producer Jody Stephens who has played drums in American rock band Big Star (with Alex Chilton of the Box Tops). Three of Big Star's studio albums are included in Rolling Stone's lists of the "500 Greatest Albums of All Time". She also worked with Golden Smog (with members of the Jayhawks, and Wilco). 

1948 - Duke Robillard

 American guitarist and singer Duke Robillard. He founded the band Roomful of Blues and was a member of the Fabulous Thunderbirds, from 1990 to replace Jimmie Vaughan. He also worked with [Bob Dylan](https://www.thisdayinmusic.com/artists/bob-dylan/). 

1947 - Jim Fielder

 Jim Fielder, bassist, from jazz-rock American group Blood Sweat & Tears. They scored the 1969 US No.2 single 'Spinning Wheel', and the 1969 US No.12 single 'You've Made Me So Very Happy'. They had a US No.1 with their second album Blood, Sweat & Tears in 1968. Fielder was also the rhythm guitarist for [Frank Zappa](https://www.thisdayinmusic.com/stairway-to-heaven/frank-zappa)'s band The Mothers of Invention in 1966 and also worked with Buffalo Springfield and Tim Buckley. 

1944 - Marlena Davis

 Marlena Davis from the American R&B group The Orlons. In 1962, the group provided back-up vocals for Dee Dee Sharp's hits 'Mashed Potato Time' and 'Gravy (For My Mashed Potatoes). They later found fame with their first national hit, 'The Wah-Watusi', which reached No. 2 in the US pop chart and which triggered the brief Watusi dance craze. Davis lost a battle with lung cancer aged 48 on 27 February 1993. 

1937 - Lloyd Green

 American steel guitarist Lloyd Green. He is noted for his extensive country music recording session career in Nashville, performing on 116 No.1 country hits, including Tammy Wynette's 'D-I-V-O-R-C-E' (1968), Charlie Rich's 'Behind Closed Doors' (1973), The Oak Ridge Boys’ 'Elvira (1981), and Alan Jackson's 'Remember When' (2003). Green was one of an inner circle of elite recording studio musicians known colloquially as the Nashville A-Team. In a career beginning in the mid-1960s Green has performed on more than 5000 recordings. 

1929 - Leroy Van Dyke

 American country music and honky-tonk singer and guitarist Leroy Van Dyke. In 1961 he had a No.1 US country hit and No.5 pop hit with 'Walk On By'. He had two other top-ten country hits, 'Auctioneer' and 'If A Woman Answers'.

## Today in Music History: Remembering Leonard Cohen

November 07, 2017

Save

![Image 3: Leonard Cohen's new album, Popular Problems, comes out Sept. 23.](https://img.apmcdn.org/de274a40ecad912fd2968def061b4de6f8b32cd9/uncropped/75e62c-20140915-leonard-cohen.jpg)

Leonard Cohen's new album, Popular Problems, comes out Sept. 23.Courtesy the artist

**History Highlight:**

Today in 2016, Canadian singer, songwriter and poet Leonard Cohen died at the age of 82 at his home in Los Angeles. Cohen pursued a career as a poet and novelist during the 1950s and early 1960s, and did not launch a music career until 1967, at the age of 33. His first album, _Songs of Leonard Cohen_ (1967), was followed by three more albums of folk music: _Songs from a Room_, _Songs of Love and Hate_ and _New Skin for the Old Ceremony_. "Hallelujah" is a song written by Cohen, originally released on his album _Various Positions_. The song found greater popular acclaim through a recording by John Cale, which inspired a recording by Jeff Buckley.

**Today In:**

1951 - Frank Sinatra married his second wife, actress Ava Gardner. The couple split up in 1953 and divorced in 1957. Sinatra was married three other times - to his first wife Nancy Barbato, to the actress Mia Farrow and finally to Barbara Marx, to whom he was married at his death.

1958 - Eddie Cochran made his U.K. chart debut with "Summertime Blues". It reached No.18 in the U.K. & No.8 in the U.S. The song has been covered by many artists, including being a No. 1 hit for country singer Alan Jackson and a notable hit for The Who.

1963 - The Beatles went to Ireland to make their only two appearances ever in the country playing two shows at the Adelphi Cinema, Dublin.

1967 - The Beatles finished recording "Blue Jay Way", "Flying" and "Magical Mystery Tour".

1968 - After Jim Morrison exhorted the audience to stand up at a concert, The Doors were banned in Phoenix because the local authorities were nervous. He had recently mooned an audience at another concert.

1969 - The Rolling Stones opened their first U.S. concert tour in three years. By this time they were notorious bad boys after tales of drug busts, censorship battles and wild life on the road, so the tour had become a full-blown media circus.

1974 - Ted Nugent won the National Squirrel Shooting Archery Contest by hitting a squirrel at 150 yards with a bow and arrow.  
  
1975 - A new world record was set for continuous guitar string plucking by a guy named Steve Anderson, who played for 114 hours 17 minutes.

1975 - Elton John started a three-week run at No. 1 on the U.S. album chart with _Rock Of The Westies_, the singer's tenth studio album and seventh U.S. No. 1.

1977 - the soundtrack to _Saturday Night Fever_ was released. The film has been citied as the first example of "cross-media marketing", with the tie-in soundtrack's single being used to help promote the film _before_ its release and the film popularizing the entire soundtrack _after_ its release.

1981 - Hall and Oates started a two-week run at No. 1 on the U.S. singles chart with "Private Eyes", the duo's third U.S. No. 1, a No. 32 hit in the U.K.

1987 - Tiffany became the youngest act to score a U.S. No. 1 since Michael Jackson ("Ben", in 1972) with "I Think We're Alone Now". The song written by Ritchie Cordell was initially a 1967 hit for Tommy James & the Shondells. Fun fact: Tiffany hated the idea of recording a version of her own for her album because she thought the song wasn't modern or hip enough.

2014 - Two wealthy fans paid $300,000 to eat lasagne with Bruce Springsteen at his house. Springsteen started off the annual Stand Up For Heroes event by playing an acoustic set, then offering the instrument to the highest bidder. When bidding reached $60,000, he threw in a guitar lesson, which someone offered $250,000 for. At this point, he offered up a lasagne dinner at his house, a ride around the block in the sidecar of his motorbike and the shirt off of his back. All the money went to the Bob Woodruff Foundation, which helps injured servicemen and their families when they return home.

**Birthdays:**

Joni Mitchell is 74.

Robin Finck of Nine Inch Nails and Guns N' Roses is 46.

Lorde is 21.

[![Image 13: Devia tenir uns vuit anys, quan vau venir a la Festa Major de Pineda. Veure-us en directe, va suposar un impacte tan enorme que vaig estar emocionalment tocada durant tota una setmana. Ho recordo com si fos avui. Aquella nena que va anar a l’envelat de la plaça dels “columpios” a escoltar-vos, anys més tard es va trobar asseguda davant vostre, al despatx de Santa Elionor número 3. Gestmusic. TV3 us havia encarregat el programa d’estiu i s’havien d’enregistrar vuit programes en dos dies. Amb vosaltres a la fi del món. No vam anar a la fi del món, però sí a un plató de Bilbao per raons que ara no vénen al cas. Mentre tu, Mainat, em “recitaves” el guió de cada presentació i jo me l’aprenia de memòria, la Rosa Español m’entaforava els vestits. Acte seguit, sortia disparada al set a enregistrar la presentació de torn. Així durant dos dies. Anys més tard, estimat Toni, un bon dia em vas trucar per proposar-me dirigir una acadèmia d’alt rendiment per a cantants. La resta, ja és història i tots els que em llegiu ara, ja la coneixeu. Conèixer-vos, treballar plegats i aprendre de vosaltres, m’ha marcat més del que mai podreu imaginar. Al vostre costat vaig aprendre que la pressió es més bona de dur amb sentit de l’humor. Que cal cuidar els equips i conjugar el verb “relativitzar” quan sembla que tens un cert èxit. I que els projectes que puguis fer a la vida, per importants que et semblin, no ho són tant. Ara bé, de tots els moments que vam viure plegats, em quedo amb aquest. La Trinca novament junts, cantant… “Ja em puc morir”, vaig pensar aquell dia. Sempre us estaré agraïda. # Luciano Pavarotti facts: Opera singer's wife, children, career and death explained

24 December 2021, 12:30 | Updated: 19 January 2022, 16:52

![Image 3: Luciano Pavarotti in 1996](link_26)

![Image 4](https://cdn.tagdeliver.com/cipt/a/nobrand-dark.svg)About our ads![Image 5](https://cdn.tagdeliver.com/cipt/a/close-dark.svg)Close this ad

 Luciano Pavarotti in 1996.  Picture: [Getty](link_27)

[![Image 6: Facebook share](https://www.smoothradio.com/assets_v4r/gusto/img/facebook-share.png)](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?href=www.smoothradio.com%2Fnews%2Fmusic%2Fluciano-pavarotti-facts-wife-children-son-death%2F&app_id=233524320165894 [link_28])

If there's one person you picture when you think of opera, chances are it's Luciano Pavarotti.

The Italian operatic tenor was one of the few in his genre to successfully crossover into popular music, thanks to his incredible voice and magnetic presence on stage.

Pavarotti was one of the most celebrated tenors of all time, achieving worldwide fame and earning the title 'King of the High Cs'.

*   [**When George Michael and Pavarotti sang a spine-tingling duet of 'Don't Let The Sun Go Down On Me'**](link_29)
*   [**When Aretha Franklin had to sing ‘Nessun Dorma’ after Pavarotti fell sick at the Grammys, and it was astonishing**](link_30)

As one of the Three Tenors, he found a whole new audience when they performed their first concert during the 1990 FIFA World Cup. His most famous performance was that of 'Nessum Dorma', which became his signature song.

Pavarotti sold over 100 million records, with the first Three Tenors recording becoming the best-selling classical album of all time.

He was also known for his charity work on behalf of refugees and the Red Cross, and he often collaborated with many other artists from a variety of genres.

1.   ## Where was Luciano Pavarotti born and what did he look like as a young man?

![Image 7: Pavarotti in 1966](link_31)

 Pavarotti in 1966.  Picture: [Getty](link_32)

Luciano Pavarotti was born in 1935 near Modena in Northern Italy.

His parents were Fernando Pavarotti, a baker and amateur tenor, and Adele Venturi, a cigar factory worker.

    *   [**Brian May singing duet with Pavarotti on 'Too Much Love Will Kill You' is spectacular**](link_33)
    *   [**Watch Bryan Adams sing with Pavarotti in a spine-tingling forgotten duet**](link_34)

His family were poor, and shared a tiny two-room apartment. Pavarotti later said that his father had a fine tenor voice but rejected a singing career because of nervousness.

![Image 8](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/cWc7vYjgnTs/hqdefault.jpg)

Luciano Pavarotti sings "Nessun dorma" from Turandot (The Three Tenors in Concert 1994)

After abandoning a dream of becoming a football goalkeeper, Pavarotti spent seven years in vocal training. His earliest musical influences were his father's records, including tenors Beniamino Gigli, Giovanni Martinelli, Tito Schipa, and Enrico Caruso.

Pavarotti began studying music in 1954 aged 19 with Arrigo Pola, a respected teacher and professional tenor in Modena.

In 1955, he became a member of the Corale Rossini, a male voice choir from Modena that also included his father, and they won first prize at the International Eisteddfod in Llangollen, Wales.

He later said that this was the most important experience of his life, leading him to pursue a career in music professionally.

2.   ## Who was Luciano Pavarotti's wife?

![Image 9: Luciano Pavarotti with first wife Adua Veroni in 1987](link_35)

 Luciano Pavarotti with first wife Adua Veroni in 1987.  Picture: [Getty](link_36)

Pavarotti was married twice.

He was first married to Adua Veroni from 1961 to 2000.

In December 2003, he married his former personal assistant, Nicoletta Mantovani.

3.   ## How many children did Luciano Pavarotti have?

![Image 10: Luciano Pavarotti with his family (L-R: Cristina Pavarotti, Adua Veroni, Lorenza Pavarotti, Luciano Pavarotti, Giuliana Pavarotti, actress Jacqueline Bisset)](link_37)

 Luciano Pavarotti with his family (L-R: Cristina Pavarotti, Adua Veroni, Lorenza Pavarotti, Luciano Pavarotti, Giuliana Pavarotti, actress Jacqueline Bisset).  Picture: [Getty](link_38)

With his first wife Adua, he had three daughters: Lorenza, Cristina, and Giuliana.

He also had another daughter, Alice, with second wife Nicoletta. Alice's twin brother, Riccardo, was stillborn after complications in January 2003.

![Image 11: Luciano Pavarotti poses holding his daughter Alice, with his wife Nicoletta Mantovani](link_39)

 Luciano Pavarotti poses holding his daughter Alice, with his wife Nicoletta Mantovani.  Picture: [Getty](link_40)

![Image 12: Daughter Alice with mother Nicoletta in 2021](link_41)

 Daughter Alice with mother Nicoletta in 2021.  Picture: [Getty](link_42)

4.   ## What was Pavarotti's cause of death and how old was he?

![Image 13: Luciano Pavarotti in 2006](link_43)

 Luciano Pavarotti in 2006.  Picture: [Getty](link_44)

While embarking on an international 'farewell tour', Pavarotti was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in July 2006.

He underwent major abdominal surgery, but he died at his home in Modena on September 6, 2007. He was aged 71.

After his death, his manager Terri Robson stated: "The Maestro fought a long, tough battle against the pancreatic cancer which eventually took his life. In fitting with the approach that characterised his life and work, he remained positive until finally succumbing to the last stages of his illness".

Pavarotti's funeral was held at Modena Cathedral. Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Kofi Annan were in attendance, while the Frecce Tricolori, the aerobatic demonstration team of the Italian Air Force, flew overhead.

# Luciano Pavarotti facts: Opera singer's wife, children, career and death explained

24 December 2021, 12:30 | Updated: 19 January 2022, 16:52

![Image 3: Luciano Pavarotti in 1996](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278644?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=pHjxhpJkMsOdl6uc2nWeymuLtAo=)

![Image 4](https://cdn.tagdeliver.com/cipt/a/nobrand-dark.svg)About our ads![Image 5](https://cdn.tagdeliver.com/cipt/a/close-dark.svg)Close this ad

 Luciano Pavarotti in 1996.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/1180226370)

[![Image 6: Facebook share](https://www.smoothradio.com/assets_v4r/gusto/img/facebook-share.png)](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?href=www.smoothradio.com%2Fnews%2Fmusic%2Fluciano-pavarotti-facts-wife-children-son-death%2F&app_id=233524320165894)

If there's one person you picture when you think of opera, chances are it's Luciano Pavarotti.

The Italian operatic tenor was one of the few in his genre to successfully crossover into popular music, thanks to his incredible voice and magnetic presence on stage.

Pavarotti was one of the most celebrated tenors of all time, achieving worldwide fame and earning the title 'King of the High Cs'.

*   [**When George Michael and Pavarotti sang a spine-tingling duet of 'Don't Let The Sun Go Down On Me'**](https://www.smoothradio.com/artists/george-michael/pavarotti-duet-dont-let-the-sun-go-down-on-me/)
*   [**When Aretha Franklin had to sing ‘Nessun Dorma’ after Pavarotti fell sick at the Grammys, and it was astonishing**](https://www.smoothradio.com/artists/aretha-franklin/nessun-dorma-pavarotti-grammy-awards-1998-video/)

As one of the Three Tenors, he found a whole new audience when they performed their first concert during the 1990 FIFA World Cup. His most famous performance was that of 'Nessum Dorma', which became his signature song.

Pavarotti sold over 100 million records, with the first Three Tenors recording becoming the best-selling classical album of all time.

He was also known for his charity work on behalf of refugees and the Red Cross, and he often collaborated with many other artists from a variety of genres.

1.   ## Where was Luciano Pavarotti born and what did he look like as a young man?

![Image 7: Pavarotti in 1966](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278647?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=UkgRDH1Ey_yVfqPdNRKxarDWJec=)

 Pavarotti in 1966.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/143899736)

Luciano Pavarotti was born in 1935 near Modena in Northern Italy.

His parents were Fernando Pavarotti, a baker and amateur tenor, and Adele Venturi, a cigar factory worker.

    *   [**Brian May singing duet with Pavarotti on 'Too Much Love Will Kill You' is spectacular**](https://www.smoothradio.com/artists/queen/brian-may-duet-pavarotti-video-2003/)
    *   [**Watch Bryan Adams sing with Pavarotti in a spine-tingling forgotten duet**](https://www.smoothradio.com/artists/bryan-adams/watch-sing-pavarotti-duet/)

His family were poor, and shared a tiny two-room apartment. Pavarotti later said that his father had a fine tenor voice but rejected a singing career because of nervousness.

![Image 8](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/cWc7vYjgnTs/hqdefault.jpg)

Luciano Pavarotti sings "Nessun dorma" from Turandot (The Three Tenors in Concert 1994)

After abandoning a dream of becoming a football goalkeeper, Pavarotti spent seven years in vocal training. His earliest musical influences were his father's records, including tenors Beniamino Gigli, Giovanni Martinelli, Tito Schipa, and Enrico Caruso.

Pavarotti began studying music in 1954 aged 19 with Arrigo Pola, a respected teacher and professional tenor in Modena.

In 1955, he became a member of the Corale Rossini, a male voice choir from Modena that also included his father, and they won first prize at the International Eisteddfod in Llangollen, Wales.

He later said that this was the most important experience of his life, leading him to pursue a career in music professionally.

2.   ## Who was Luciano Pavarotti's wife?

![Image 9: Luciano Pavarotti with first wife Adua Veroni in 1987](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278652?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=nQKHEMhe8uepG3PZxnQ_i9vsa8I=)

 Luciano Pavarotti with first wife Adua Veroni in 1987.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/174302916)

Pavarotti was married twice.

He was first married to Adua Veroni from 1961 to 2000.

In December 2003, he married his former personal assistant, Nicoletta Mantovani.

3.   ## How many children did Luciano Pavarotti have?

![Image 10: Luciano Pavarotti with his family (L-R: Cristina Pavarotti, Adua Veroni, Lorenza Pavarotti, Luciano Pavarotti, Giuliana Pavarotti, actress Jacqueline Bisset)](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278649?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=f7Nj6y2sZmv1Yw9_VIGgdB5LmjY=)

 Luciano Pavarotti with his family (L-R: Cristina Pavarotti, Adua Veroni, Lorenza Pavarotti, Luciano Pavarotti, Giuliana Pavarotti, actress Jacqueline Bisset).  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/975339720)

With his first wife Adua, he had three daughters: Lorenza, Cristina, and Giuliana.

He also had another daughter, Alice, with second wife Nicoletta. Alice's twin brother, Riccardo, was stillborn after complications in January 2003.

![Image 11: Luciano Pavarotti poses holding his daughter Alice, with his wife Nicoletta Mantovani](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278650?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=zHS9JfCL26nLJOnmBqJeIVLUdsI=)

 Luciano Pavarotti poses holding his daughter Alice, with his wife Nicoletta Mantovani.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/158745832)

![Image 12: Daughter Alice with mother Nicoletta in 2021](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278651?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=YIM5s5pf2-vHUQ6cIcnO1qVJu7k=)

 Daughter Alice with mother Nicoletta in 2021.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/1354936627)

4.   ## What was Pavarotti's cause of death and how old was he?

![Image 13: Luciano Pavarotti in 2006](https://imgs.smoothradio.com/images/278648?crop=16_9&width=660&relax=1&format=webp&signature=HyYQelNjzsCdVLIaQTvEnSuskvc=)

 Luciano Pavarotti in 2006.  Picture: [Getty](https://www.gettyimages.co.uk/license/115434025)

While embarking on an international 'farewell tour', Pavarotti was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in July 2006.

He underwent major abdominal surgery, but he died at his home in Modena on September 6, 2007. He was aged 71.

After his death, his manager Terri Robson stated: "The Maestro fought a long, tough battle against the pancreatic cancer which eventually took his life. In fitting with the approach that characterised his life and work, he remained positive until finally succumbing to the last stages of his illness".

Pavarotti's funeral was held at Modena Cathedral. Prime Minister Romano Prodi and Kofi Annan were in attendance, while the Frecce Tricolori, the aerobatic demonstration team of the Italian Air Force, flew overhead.

**Luciano Pavarotti**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-1) (12 October 1935–6 September 2007) was an Italian operatic [tenor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor "Tenor") who during the late part of his career crossed over into [popular music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music"), eventually becoming one of the most acclaimed tenors of all time. He made numerous recordings of complete [operas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opera "Opera") and individual [arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), gaining worldwide fame for his tone and the [nickname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorific_nicknames_in_popular_music "Honorific nicknames in popular music") "King of the [High Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_C "High C")".

As one of [the Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Three_Tenors "The Three Tenors"), who performed their first concert during the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") before a global audience, Pavarotti became well known for his televised concerts and media appearances. From the beginning of his professional career as a tenor in 1961 in Italy to his final performance of "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" at the [2006 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Winter_Olympics "2006 Winter Olympics") in [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), Pavarotti was at his best in [bel canto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bel_canto "Bel canto") operas, pre-_[Aida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aida "Aida")_[Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi") roles, and [Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini") works such as _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_, _[Tosca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tosca "Tosca")_, _[Turandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turandot "Turandot")_ and _[Madama Butterfly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madama\_Butterfly "Madama Butterfly")_. He sold more than 100 million records,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-2) and the [first Three Tenors recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras_Domingo_Pavarotti_in_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert") became the best-selling classical album of all time. Pavarotti was also noted for his charity work on behalf of [refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refugee "Refugee") and the [Red Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Red_Cross_and_Red_Crescent_Movement "International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement"), amongst others. He was appointed a [Knight Grand Cross of the Order of Merit of the Italian Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Merit_of_the_Italian_Republic "Order of Merit of the Italian Republic") in 1988.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-3) Pavarotti died from [pancreatic cancer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") on 6 September 2007.

## Biography

### Early life and musical training

Luciano Pavarotti was born on 12 October 1935 in a public housing block on the outskirts of [Modena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modena "Modena") in [Northern Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Italy "Northern Italy"), the son of Fernando Pavarotti, a baker and amateur tenor, and Adele Venturi, a cigar factory worker.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-5) Although he spoke fondly of his childhood, the family had little money; its four members were crowded into a two-room apartment. According to Pavarotti, his father had a fine tenor voice but rejected the possibility of a singing career because of nervousness. [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") forced the family out of the city in 1943. For the following year, they rented a single room from a farmer in the neighbouring countryside, where the young Pavarotti developed an interest in farming.

After abandoning the dream of becoming a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football")[goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), Pavarotti spent seven years in vocal training. Pavarotti's earliest musical influences were his father's records, most of them featuring the popular tenors of the day—[Beniamino Gigli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beniamino_Gigli "Beniamino Gigli"), [Giovanni Martinelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Martinelli "Giovanni Martinelli"), [Tito Schipa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tito_Schipa "Tito Schipa"), and [Enrico Caruso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrico_Caruso "Enrico Caruso").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) Pavarotti's favourite tenor and idol was [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) He was also deeply influenced by [Mario Lanza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Lanza "Mario Lanza"), saying: "In my teens I used to go to Mario Lanza movies and then come home and imitate him in the mirror". At around the age of nine, he began singing with his father in a small local church choir.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

In addition to music, as a child, Pavarotti enjoyed playing [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"). When he graduated from the Scuola Magistrale, he was interested in pursuing a career as a professional football [goalkeeper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goalkeeper_(association_football) "Goalkeeper (association football)"), but his mother convinced him to train as a teacher. He subsequently taught in an elementary school for two years but finally decided to pursue a music career. His father, recognising the risk involved, only reluctantly gave his consent. Pavarotti began the serious study of music in 1954 at the age of 19 with [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), a respected teacher and professional tenor in Modena who offered to teach him without remuneration. According to conductor [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge"), Pavarotti never learned to read music.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-6)

In 1955, he experienced his first singing success when he was a member of the Corale Rossini, a [male voice choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Male_voice_choir "Male voice choir") from Modena that also included his father, which won first prize at the [International Eisteddfod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen_International_Musical_Eisteddfod "Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod") in [Llangollen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Llangollen "Llangollen"), Wales. He later said that this was the most important experience of his life, and that it inspired him to become a professional singer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-7)

When his teacher, [Arrigo Pola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrigo_Pola "Arrigo Pola"), moved to Japan, Pavarotti became a student of [Ettore Campogalliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ettore_Campogalliani "Ettore Campogalliani"), who at that time was also teaching Pavarotti's childhood friend, [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni"), whose mother worked with Luciano's mother in the cigar factory. Like Pavarotti, Freni went on to become a successful opera singer; they collaborated in various stage performances and recordings together.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

During his years of musical study, Pavarotti held part-time jobs to sustain himself—first as an elementary school teacher and then as an insurance salesman. The first six years of study resulted in only a few recitals, all in small towns and without pay. When a [nodule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_fold_nodule "Vocal fold nodule") developed on his [vocal cords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_folds "Vocal folds"), causing a _"disastrous"_ concert in [Ferrara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrara "Ferrara"), he decided to give up singing. Pavarotti attributed his immediate improvement to the psychological release connected with this decision. Whatever the reason, the nodule not only disappeared but, as he related in his autobiography: "Everything I had learned came together with my natural voice to make the sound I had been struggling so hard to achieve".

### Career: 1960s–1970s

Pavarotti began his career as a tenor in smaller regional Italian opera houses. After winning the Achille Peri International Competition, he made his debut as Rodolfo in _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ at the [Teatro Municipale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teatro_Municipale_di_Reggio "Teatro Municipale di Reggio") in [Reggio Emilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Emilia "Reggio Emilia") in April 1961, conducted by [Francesco Molinari-Pradelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Molinari-Pradelli "Francesco Molinari-Pradelli") and staged by [Mafalda Favero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mafalda_Favero "Mafalda Favero").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4) His first known recording of "[Che gelida manina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Che_gelida_manina "Che gelida manina")" was recorded during this performance.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-8)

In December 1961, Pavarotti made his first international appearance in _[La traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_traviata "La traviata")_ in [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"), [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-10) On 23 February 1963, he debuted at the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") in the same role. In March and April 1963, Pavarotti performed again in Vienna as Rodolfo and as Duca di Mantova in _[Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto")_. The same year, he performed his first solo non-opera concert outside Italy when he sang in [Dundalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundalk "Dundalk"), Ireland, for the St Cecilia's Gramophone Society.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) He was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing The Duke of Mantua in Verdi's [Rigoletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rigoletto "Rigoletto") in May and June,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-dundalk-11) and his [Royal Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Royal_Opera "The Royal Opera") debut, where he replaced an indisposed [Giuseppe Di Stefano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Di_Stefano "Giuseppe Di Stefano") as Rodolfo.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-13) In September 1963, he made his debut at Covent Garden in La Boheme, which gave his career a boost.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-14)

In 1964, Pavarotti appeared as Idamante in _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_ at [Glyndebourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glyndebourne_Festival_Opera "Glyndebourne Festival Opera")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-15) and was engaged by the Dublin Grand Opera Society to sing Rodolfo in [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[La bohème](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_boh%C3%A8me "La bohème")_ and Alfredo in Giuseppe Verdi's _[La Traviata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_Traviata "La Traviata")_. Reviewers favourably comment on his singing.

Pavarotti sang with Joan Sutherland when he made his American début with the [Greater Miami Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida_Grand_Opera "Florida Grand Opera") in February 1965, singing in [Gaetano Donizetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaetano_Donizetti "Gaetano Donizetti")'s _[Lucia di Lammermoor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucia\_di\_Lammermoor "Lucia di Lammermoor")_ on the stage of the [Miami-Dade County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami-Dade_County "Miami-Dade County") Auditorium in Miami. The tenor that was scheduled to perform that night became ill with no understudy. Sutherland recommended Pavarotti as he was acquainted with the role. On 28 April, Pavarotti made his [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala") debut in the revival of the [Franco Zeffirelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco_Zeffirelli "Franco Zeffirelli") production of _La bohème_, with his childhood friend [Mirella Freni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirella_Freni "Mirella Freni") singing Mimi and [Herbert von Karajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_von_Karajan "Herbert von Karajan") conducting. Karajan had requested the singer's engagement.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

[Joan Sutherland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Sutherland "Joan Sutherland") and her conductor husband, [Richard Bonynge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bonynge "Richard Bonynge") sought a tall tenor to take along on their 1965 tour to Australia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-aboutvoice-12) During the Australia tour in summer 1965, Sutherland and Pavarotti sang forty performances over two months. Pavarotti later credited Sutherland for the breathing and diaphragm technique that sustained him through his career.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

After the extended Australian tour, he returned to La Scala, where he added Tebaldo from _[I Capuleti e i Montecchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Capuleti\_e\_i\_Montecchi "I Capuleti e i Montecchi")_ to his repertoire on 26 March 1966, with [Giacomo Aragall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Aragall "Giacomo Aragall") as Romeo.

His first appearance as Tonio in Donizetti's _[La fille du régiment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La\_fille\_du\_r%C3%A9giment "La fille du régiment")_ took place at the Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, on 2 June 1966. In this performance, he was the first tenor to deliver nine natural high Cs in the aria "Ah! mes amis".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-tenor-4)

He scored another major triumph in Rome on 20 November 1969 when he sang in _[I Lombardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I\_Lombardi\_alla\_prima\_crociata "I Lombardi alla prima crociata")_ opposite [Renata Scotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renata_Scotto "Renata Scotto"). This was recorded on a private label and widely distributed, as were various recordings of his _I Capuleti e i Montecchi_, usually with Aragall. Early commercial recordings included a recital of Donizetti (the aria from _[Don Sebastiano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom\_S%C3%A9bastien "Dom Sébastien")_ were particularly highly regarded) and [Verdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giuseppe_Verdi "Giuseppe Verdi")[arias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria"), as well as a complete _[L'elisir d'amore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L'elisir\_d'amore "L'elisir d'amore")_ with Sutherland.

His breakthrough in the United States came on 17 February 1972, in a production of _La fille du régiment_ at New York's [Metropolitan Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Opera "Metropolitan Opera"), in which he hit nine [high Cs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenor_C "Tenor C") in the signature [aria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aria "Aria") and had seventeen curtain calls.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-16) This earned him the nickname "King of the High Cs".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-17)

Pavarotti sang his international [recital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert#Recital "Concert") début at [William Jewell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Jewell_College "William Jewell College") in [Liberty, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty,_Missouri "Liberty, Missouri"), on 1 February 1973, as part of the college's Fine Arts Program, now known as the Harriman–Jewell Series.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) According to his manager at the time, Pavarotti clutched a handkerchief throughout this recital because he had a lingering cold.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-19) Pavarotti himself explained that he needed the handkerchief, since he didn't know what to do with his hands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-:0-18) The prop became a signature part of his solo performances.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-20) He began to give frequent television performances, starting with his performances as Rodolfo (_La bohème_) in the first [Live from the Met](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live_from_the_Met "Live from the Met") telecast in March 1977, which attracted one of the largest audiences ever for a televised opera.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-21) He won [Grammy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Award "Grammy Award") awards and [platinum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platinum_disc "Platinum disc") and [gold discs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_disc "Gold disc") for his performances.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1976, Pavarotti debuted at the [Salzburg Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salzburg_Festival "Salzburg Festival"), appearing in a solo recital on 31 July, accompanied by pianist Leone Magiera. Pavarotti returned to the festival in 1978 with a recital and as the Italian singer in _[Der Rosenkavalier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der\_Rosenkavalier "Der Rosenkavalier")_ in 1983 with _[Idomeneo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idomeneo "Idomeneo")_, and both in 1985 and 1988 with solo recitals. In 1979, he was profiled in a cover story in the weekly magazine _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-22) That same year saw Pavarotti's return to the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") after an absence of fourteen years. With Herbert von Karajan conducting, Pavarotti sang Manrico in _[Il trovatore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Il\_trovatore "Il trovatore")_. In 1978, he appeared in a solo recital on _[Live from Lincoln Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_from\_Lincoln\_Center "Live from Lincoln Center")_.

### Career: 1980s–1990s

At the beginning of the 1980s, he set up The Pavarotti International Voice Competition for young singers, performing with the winners in 1982 in excerpts of _La bohème_ and _L'elisir d'amore_. The second competition, in 1986, staged excerpts of _La bohème_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. To celebrate the 25th anniversary of his career, he brought the winners of the competition to Italy for gala performances of _La bohème_ in Modena and [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genoa "Genoa"), and then to China, where they staged performances of _La bohème_ in Beijing ([Peking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peking "Peking")). To conclude the visit, Pavarotti performed the inaugural concert in the [Great Hall of the People](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Hall_of_the_People "Great Hall of the People") before 10,000 people, receiving a [standing ovation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_ovation "Standing ovation") for nine high Cs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-24) The third competition in 1989 again staged performances of _L'elisir d'amore_ and _Un ballo in maschera_. The winners of the fifth competition accompanied Pavarotti in performances in [Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia "Philadelphia") in 1997.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In the mid-1980s, Pavarotti returned to two opera houses that had provided him with important breakthroughs, the [Vienna State Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_State_Opera "Vienna State Opera") and [La Scala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Scala "La Scala"). Vienna saw Pavarotti as Rodolfo in _La bohème_ with [Carlos Kleiber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Kleiber "Carlos Kleiber") conducting, and again Mirella Freni was Mimi; as Nemorino in _L'elisir d'amore_; as Radames in _Aida_ conducted by Lorin Maazel; as Rodolfo in _Luisa Miller_; and as Gustavo in _Un ballo in maschera_ conducted by Claudio Abbado. In 1996, Pavarotti appeared for the last time at the Staatsoper in _Andrea Chénier_. Throughout the 1980s and 90s, promoters [Tibor Rudas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibor_Rudas "Tibor Rudas") and [Harvey Goldsmith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvey_Goldsmith "Harvey Goldsmith") booked Pavarotti into increasingly larger venues.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1985, Pavarotti sang Radames at La Scala opposite Maria Chiara in a Luca Ronconi production conducted by Maazel, recorded on video. His performance of the aria "Celeste Aida" received a two-minute ovation on the opening night.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] He was reunited with Mirella Freni for the San Francisco Opera production of _La bohème_ in 1988, also recorded on video. In 1992, La Scala saw Pavarotti in a new Zeffirelli production of _Don Carlos_, conducted by Riccardo Muti.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-25)

Pavarotti became even better known throughout the world in 1990 when his rendition of the aria "[Nessun dorma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nessun_dorma "Nessun dorma")" from [Giacomo Puccini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giacomo_Puccini "Giacomo Puccini")'s _[Turandot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turandot "Turandot")_ was taken as the theme song of [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s coverage of the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") in Italy. The aria achieved pop status, became the World Cup soundtrack, and remained his trademark song.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-26) This was followed by the first [Three Tenors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Tenors "Three Tenors") concert, held on the eve of the [1990 FIFA World Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup_Final "1990 FIFA World Cup Final") at the ancient [Baths of Caracalla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baths_of_Caracalla "Baths of Caracalla") in Rome with fellow tenors [Plácido Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pl%C3%A1cido_Domingo "Plácido Domingo") and [José Carreras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Carreras "José Carreras") and conductor [Zubin Mehta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zubin_Mehta "Zubin Mehta"). The performance for the World Cup closing concert captivated a global audience, and it became the biggest-selling classical record of all time.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-27) A highlight of the concert, in which Pavarotti sang the opening verses using extended vocal runs for di Capua's "['O sole mio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/'O_sole_mio "'O sole mio")" and which was in turn perfectly repeated note-for-note by Domingo and Carreras. The recorded album sold millions of copies,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-28) and the [first Three Tenors recording](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carreras_Domingo_Pavarotti_in_Concert "Carreras Domingo Pavarotti in Concert") became the best-selling classical album of all time.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-29) Throughout the 1990s, Pavarotti appeared in outdoor concerts, [including his televised concert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pavarotti_in_the_Park "Pavarotti in the Park") in London's [Hyde Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyde_Park,_London "Hyde Park, London"), which drew a record attendance of 150,000. In June 1993, more than 500,000 listeners gathered for his free performance on the Great Lawn of New York's [Central Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Park "Central Park"), while millions more around the world watched on television.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-30) The following September, in the shadow of the [Eiffel Tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower "Eiffel Tower") in Paris, he sang for an estimated crowd of 300,000.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-31) Following on from the original 1990 concert, the Three Tenors concerts were held during the three subsequent [FIFA World Cup Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_FIFA_World_Cup_finals "List of FIFA World Cup finals"), in 1994 in Los Angeles, 1998 in Paris, and 2002 in Yokohama.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciano_Pavarotti#cite_note-FIFA-32)
